speaker: markbennett
text: Okay, Councillors, we're live at the moment. Firstly to anybody who's watching the broadcast tonight, my apologies, we've had a technical issue here. We're a little late starting, so welcome to this ordinary meeting of Hunters Hill Council number 4481. I'd like to acknowledge the traditional custodians of the land on which we meet and the waters that surround us, and I pay my respect to their elders past and present. We thank you, Lord, for the honour of being called by our fellow citizens to this office of honour and trust. Give us grace, diligently and honourably, free from private interest or prejudice, to discharge the duties entrusted to us, to the common good, and as in your sight, through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen. Thank you. I don't think we have any apologies this evening. Are there any declarations of interest? We'll move on to the minutes of the previous meeting. Move Councillor Williams, seconded Councillor McLACHLAN. Any discussion required, Councillors? I'll put those in favour. Against. That's carried. Thank you. Are there any matters arising out of those minutes?

speaker: bencollins
text: Councillor COLLINS. Councillor COLLINS. I just have a non-pecuniary, non-significant interest, sorry, that I missed in 4.6.

speaker: markbennett
text: Thank you, Councillor COLLINS. Okay, Councillors, we have an item which is in the agenda, which is item 4.7, licence agreements for the Happy Hens, which is 4.7. Suggestion that we move it forward. Councillor MILES, Councillor Williams will bring 4.7 forward, and we have some speakers for that. Just one moment, Councillors. We have a supporter in a question who says, dear Mayor, Councillors, an amazing, hard-working staff have come to your Council. From the Happy Hens, a huge thank you to you all for believing in us. In 2018, we came to you with a plan for using part of a disused bowling green at Henley Community Centre. We wanted to create an edible garden for our community. We had Bedlam Bay Community Garden up and running, however, we needed more space. Council worked forward-thinking and allowed us half of one of the old bowling greens at Henley for two years from 3 August 2018. Henley Green Community Garden began. Thank you. I am thrilled to say that the dream has come to fruition, and we have a fantastic edible garden that is an asset to the local area. The Happy Hens thank Council for our peppercorn rent arrangement. We are all volunteers and are only now in a position where we can start to look at creating a sustainable income into the future. Our space at Henley is valued at $2,500 per annum in rent by Council. Using this space, the Happy Hens have raised over $65,000 of assets via federal, state and local grants, fundraisers and paid work for our volunteers, the environment, for those less able and the community at large. The Hunters Hill residents, preschool students and many others from further afield enjoy this space daily. We all thank you. Whilst it is difficult to measure smiles, we have put together some statistics for you, our benefactors at Hunters Hill Council. Henley Green currently has 32 financial members plus children and 200-plus people participating in volunteer activities between 3 August 2018 and 5 June 2020. 3,284 hours of volunteer time have been spent at Henley Green between 3 August 2018 to 15 June 2020, equating to $137,000 if the same number of hours were paid, and that comes from the ABS estimate on the per hour value of volunteer time. 38 hours per week is spent at Henley Green working on the productive garden, equating to a full-time job for one person. Volunteer hours have increased by 41.5% in the second year of operation at Henley Green. There has been a 25% increase in the number of new volunteers to the site in the second year of operation. These are all very positive signs of a solid and growing interest in the activities at Henley Green and support of our group in the community. Thank you. The Happy Hens plans to align with Hunters Hill Council's strategic objectives in the community strategic plan, with a focus on community. Along with Council, we aim to create an inclusive, connected, informed and healthy community which encompasses the wellbeing of all residents, which is CSP 2020. We feel that Council does encourage and support community groups that are inclusive, engaging and enhancing social cohesion, the Happy Hens being a case in point. We have preschoolers mixing with senior members of our community and enhancing wellbeing all round. Our coaches and abilities are welcoming at Henley, with wheelchair ramps installed, sensory aids, wheelchair-friendly tables, veggie pods raised for use by all, plus a safe, green, large area for kids to run and enjoy the outdoors while learning about where food comes from. We also aim to assist community members and Council with managing and preserving our environment. Sustainable living is important to our group and we always look to innovate and use resources that are waste to others. Our edible garden is built on recycled cardboard, our chook shed, an old, unwanted cubby house. We compost and create our own soil. Most of our edible plants are from seeds we have saved or been donated. Our newest project is our community recycling project. This is open to all and involves collecting and recycling tomato punnets, egg cartons, milk bottle tops and rings, coffee pods, glasses frames, bread tags, coffee grounds from local cafes and compostable food items from households. We look forward to Council letting their residents know this is available for all in the community. We would like to thank everyone at Hunters Hill Council for making Henley Green Community Garden a reality for all the community. We appreciate our relationship with Council and admire the hard work that Council staff have been putting in for all their community groups and residents. We thank you for the one-year lease extension and look forward to a solid partnership with Hunters Hill Council moving into the next phase for the happy hens and well into the future. Thank you all. Warm regards, Emma. Thank you, Emma Paxton. The next speaker we have is Leigh Cootman, Director of Riverside Preschool. Thank you, Mr Mayor. Also a supporter and says, to whom it may concern, over the last few years, Riverside Preschool families have enjoyed forming a strong relationship with Henley Hens Community Garden. The preschool children have been involved in a variety of rich experiences with Henley Hens, such as planting and watering the garden and garden, arts and crafts experiences to name but a few. The highlight of many preschool children's day is visiting the chickens daily to feed them, give them a pat and enthusiastically collect eggs the chickens have laid. A lot of children request daily that they—can they go down to see the chickens. One of our families was instrumental in looking after the chickens in their home until they were big enough to handle the conditions of the outdoors. Although this family has left the preschool now, they still come back to visit the garden and chickens regularly. The children and families have been fascinated to observe the garden space flourish and love visiting the area daily to collect veggies, herbs or spend some time talking—taking a walk through the garden beds before or after preschool. The preschool children and their families have been involved in many community events at the garden, involved in morning teas to celebrate Seniors Week, Clean Up Australia events and Working Bees, all of which have brought the community together. The children are now busily involved in learning the benefits of sustainability initiatives to support the Henley Hens, learning the value of growing your own produce to recycling waste, which further extends the preschool's early childhood education. Besides all the lovely community connections this has provided, the children have benefited by having the community garden and the many learning opportunities it provides to children, learning where food comes from, developing life skills in growing and cooking food, understanding of life cycles, plants and animals, care of the earth and living things and encouraging a love of nature. Our community is looking forward to our relationship with Henley Hens to continue in the coming years and look forward to strengthening our community through shared projects and events. Kind regards, Lee Coopman, Director. Councillor CUMMING. Thank you, Lee Coopman. The next speaker will be Anne Mageehan. Anne Mageehan. Also a supporter says, dear Council, thank you for providing us with this wonderful space. I grew up on a farm in Ireland and missed the feeling of space and getting my hands dirty. I was very restricted with a small backyard that didn't get a lot of sun. This space is so important to me. It helps connect with the community. I truly can't imagine my life without it. We have a great group of volunteers with Helen, Emma and Nicole to guide us. I get some exercise and a chat with the other volunteers. We share our ideas and learn from each other. I have brought my grandchildren to the garden. They love checking out what's new. The chickens are a great source of interest with the kids checking for eggs. It is a very community-minded area and the Council's help is very much appreciated. Kind regards, Anne Mageehan. Thank you, Anne Mageehan. The next speaker is Sarah Vickers. Sarah says, dear Council, I understand that next week a continuation of the lease for Henley Green Community Garden will be discussed. I have been a regular volunteer at the garden for a number of months and believe it offers considerable benefits to the community as well as to the individuals involved. As a volunteer, the garden improves both my physical and emotional health. It enables connections and establishment of community. This is valuable to me in normal times, but especially at the moment with the limited movement and social contacts from the enforced COVID-19 conditions. With being there on Sunday afternoons, it is also a focus for local people and visitors. With people of all ages stopping for a chat to find out more, the garden is clearly aligned with Council's strategic plans with its focus on community, environmental emphasis and commitment to enabling access for all. It fits well with the village and community feel that we value so much as residents of the Hunters Hill area. I would ask that Council extend the lease and allow us to maintain this valuable community resource into the future. Best regards, Sarah Vickers. Thank you, Sarah Vickers. Our next speaker is Janet McIntosh. Thanks, Mr Mayor. Also a supporter, Janet says, support for the continuation of lease of land for Henley Green Community Garden. To whom it may concern, I first became aware of this outstanding project when I was looking to involve myself in a nearby community activity in which I could be outdoors and work with like-minded people. Over the past 15 months, I have been astounded at the dedication, determination and cohesion of this group as we strive to provide a thoughtful, plentiful and welcoming place to come together. Furthermore, I have been impressed to learn that the group not only embraces the interests in gardening and share of knowledge and harvest. It is also selflessly engaged in supporting other community activities and those in need, be it for welfare or mental health. This site for such an activity is outstanding on many, many counts, notwithstanding being a wide open area with sufficient sun to suit the purpose. Easy access with just enough privacy to deter vandalism and has access to both water and power which are essential for the project to be possible. The location of the Henley Green Community Garden provides a fantastic interest and example for the children in the adjacent preschool who are frequent visitors and are engaged in feeding and caring for the hens. On occasions, planting seeds and watching their development into beautiful plants and discovering just how the vegetables are at home start life. Frequently, visitors drop by out of curiosity and stay for a chat or share in the harvest and sometimes they return to join the team. All are amazed at the area our Henley Community Garden Group has developed and many nearby residents express their delight at how the site is being used. This project is a fine example for other councils to aspire and to provide. I strongly urge Hunters Hill Council to extend the lease of land at Henley's Green for continued use as a community garden for the foreseeable future. We thank in anticipation for the continuation of this lease. Thank you, Janet McIntosh. The next speaker we have is Pam Freeland. Thank you. Also a supporter, Pam says, Hunters Hill Council, regarding Henley Community Garden, I first met the happy hens at Lane Cove at a community sustainability event in 2019. As the local community garden had ceased operating, I took the opportunity to join their team of volunteer gardeners later in the year. I had recently moved into a unit and sorely missed my garden. I am able to do small-scale balcony gardening, but the opportunity to grow food for the community with surplus going to the Sydney Community Services appealed to me. The hens and the other gardeners were very welcoming, helpful and patient. I have learned much from them all and hope to apply some of the things I've learned in my unit block. Nearby residents, walkers and bridge players are always interested in what is going on and frequently wander over to us to ask questions about the produce and what we are doing. The pre-school children next door use the garden as a resource and even feed the chooks and collect their eggs. As an early childhood teacher, I know the value of these experiences and the knowledge of where food comes from and the interaction with the natural environment cannot be underestimated. When COVID-19 and subsequent travel restrictions hit, I reluctantly gave up my weekly sessions as I am particularly vulnerable to respiratory disease. I watched the volunteers' efforts from afar using WhatsApp and was impressed by their dedication. The careful organisation of rosters, strict hygiene and social distancing allowed the gardens to continue. I realised what I gained from the garden during my absence. Physical exercise, social interactions, mental health and a sense of doing something worthwhile, often difficult for recent retirees like me to find. I have recently returned to weekly sessions and am impressed with the vision and enthusiasm Helen, Emma and Nicole display in their care and concern for the environment and their community. I encourage the Council to continue supporting the Happy Hens community activities on this site and allow them to further engage with and involve the community in their proposed plans for the gardens. I remain yours sincerely, Pam Freeland. Thank you, Pam Freeland. The next speaker we have is Sabina Fielding-Smith. Thank you. Sabina is also a supporter and says, Dear Mayor Bennett and Huntersville Councillors, I write this letter in support of the Henley Grand Community Garden, instigated and conducted by the Happy Hens Social Enterprising. I have been involved in this group as a volunteer since its beginning in 2018, first with Bedlam Bay Community Garden and now at the site of the Henley Community Centre. The community garden at Henley is a wonderful venture, not only to grow organic fresh vegetables but also as a community hub where local and non-local residents can have meaningful connection and networking opportunities. Everyone is welcomed no matter what their skill base is because it is a place of learning, sharing and inclusion. Volunteers attending come from all walks of life, attitudes and places from around the globe. In a mutual atmosphere of sharing, kindness and tolerance, the garden has blossomed not only physically but also figuratively to encompass a lot more. The Happy Hens Social Enterprise Executive has gone to great lengths to include other community groups, including the Henley Preschool Kindergarten, Boomerang Bags 5 for Ride, as well as inviting groups from the North Ryde Business Park to experience firsthand what it is to install garden beds and grow your own food. They also have invited people with a disability from Royal Rehabilitation Centre to attend monthly bag making sessions at the garden until recently. These are placed on hold currently because of COVID-19 pandemic. I am very fortunate to be a member of this group and have the opportunity to not only grow wonderful fresh organic produce, but to find friendship and a wonderful sense of community and inclusion. I am very glad that Hunters Hill Council has given this community group an opportunity to use this old bowling green that was lying idle, a new lease of life which is a fabulous asset into the future. Yours sincerely, Sabina. Thank you to Sabina Fielding-Smith. We're very fortunate we have people like this in the community and I recall the determination when they approached Council some time ago wanting to set this up and I remember some very enthusiastic Councillors who got behind it as well. It's been great to see it doing so well. So the recommendations there, page 214, moved Councillor Miles, seconded Councillor Sanderson. Councillor Miles?

speaker: elizabethkrassoi
text: Thanks Mr. Mayor. Congratulations to the Hens two years on and they've just done so much in that short time that they've had. And I think, you know, Council through our community grants, we support a lot of community groups, some that service a few dozen people, some that through their reach service a few hundred. And it's a small grant that we offer people, but they do so much with it. So by having this, as you say, peppercorn rent agreement, we've enabled the Hens to give so much back to our community that we reap the benefits of. So I'm grateful to them. We live on the leafy North Shore. And so you would imagine a lot of people have the opportunity to stick a veggie patch somewhere in their median strip or on their small backyards. But what somewhere like a community garden brings is the skills that a lot of people don't have and therefore don't explore the opportunity of nourishing themselves from home. And they also bring the scale. So you can really do more around composting and sustainability and projects that benefit everyone. So congratulations to them for that. I was listening on the news the other day about our small local newspapers and how important they are to be the voices of local communities and how important local initiatives get lost now because some communities are missing out on that reporting from their papers. And so I think it's a good opportunity to thank the Weekly Times as well for the support they've been giving the Hens and promoting the work that they've been doing and hopefully promoting even further the partnership that they have with Council and the things they hope to achieve. On local Facebook page Love Gladesville, I noticed a couple of weeks ago someone said, do you think it would be a good idea to have a community garden here in Hunters Hill Gladesville area? And someone else responded and said, oh, my God, haven't you heard of the Happy Hens at Henley Bowling Club? So the word isn't out there enough yet. And it started a really good conversation on that particular Facebook page. So people are hankering for it. And so I think communication is key. So it's great to hear that Council are planning on doing some more promoting of their initiatives. And, of course, very excited to hear that they're venturing deeper into sustainability initiatives, which I know they're all passionate about anyway. So good things to come. And thank you, Hens.

speaker: markbennett
text: Thank you. I'm assuming there is nobody wishing to speak against the recommendations. So if you're all done, I'll put the recommendation. Those in favour? Against? That's carried. And the recommendation is the minute be received and noted and a letter of condolence be forwarded to Ron De Boyd's family. With much sadness, I advise Councillors and Council staff of the passing of Ron De Boyd at the age of 93. Ron De was a most respected citizen of Hunters Hill who was known for her commitment to others. Father Bates described her recently as being a part of the fabric of the church and of great integrity and faith, larger than life, with a warm and generous heart. The oldest alumni of Villa Maria Catholic School, Rhonda Nee Timbrel, recently shared with current Villa Maria students memories of being taught by the sisters in summers swimming in the baths her father helped build at Tarma Creek, where they used for their swimming carnivals. Rhonda was the loving wife of Arthur Boyd, who was the mayor of Hunters Hill in 1998 and 1999. She has many legacies. And on behalf of Council, I extend to Rhonda's children and children-in-law, Felicity, Martin, Gabrielle, Nicholas, Damien and their respective families, our sincere condolences, as we fondly and formally remember their dear, dearly loved mother and grandmother who contributed so much to our community. So, I'd like to move that. Do I have a seconder? Councillor Sanderson. All in favour? That's carried. Thank you very much. Another item which I'd like to deal with is a public service medal awarded to Miss Jane Winter. The recommendation is at the minute be received and noted in the letter of congratulations. We forward to Miss Jane Winter. Excuse me, Councillors. On the 8th of June, 2020, the Governor-General and Chancellor of the Order of Australia is Excellency General and Honourable David John Hurley, an early ACDC retired, recognised 933 Australians in the Queen's Birthday 2020 Honours List. Included in the list was Woolwich resident, Miss Jane Winter, who was recognised for outstanding public service to the visual arts and cultural sector in New South Wales. Miss Winter is the current Head of Philanthropy at the New South Wales Art Gallery, whose impressive array of accomplishments included raising over $26 million in her role over the last 15 years, significantly enhanced the gallery's reputation with Australia Board and assured the future health of the gallery's acquisitions fund. We congratulate Miss Winter and thank her for her contribution to the community. So, I'll move that. Do I have a seconder? Councillor Williams. All in favour? Carried, that's unanimous, thank you. So, we move to item 4.1, the adoption of the budget fees and charges long-term financial plan rates and charges. Do I have a mover? Councillor Williams. Seconded Councillor Sanderson. Councillor Williams.

speaker: rosswilliams
text: Yes, Mr. Mayor. I'm privileged to be the representative on this group and I've spent a lot of time in state government and local government, but I've never ever come across a process that has a collective of 11 councils, four state agencies all working together to achieve positive outcomes for not only the Huntersville community, but the broader Parramatta River Catchment and Sydney community. It's an outstanding master plan that they produced in the first phase of the operation. Now they're deep into delivering on that master plan through their operational plan. And the last meeting, which Jackie Volmer, the staff representative was along at, I was amazed at how much progress they've made in the contribution, which it does make not only to the broader community, but also to benefiting our community. And some of the highlights in that process is particularly the standardised standards process, which will help to clearly define objectives for councils and state government agencies to adopt regarding stormwater quality, waterways and repairing lands. And those issues are very relevant to us and I understand our staff have been working closely with this group to help develop those because it's been a collaborative effort. And it's one that I think will provide us with some very good tools to add into LEP and DCPs when we do the review process and also into the LSPS. It's an important contribution, which this group have made to what is ongoing and a long protracted issue around improving stormwater quality and its impact on our waterways and our repairing lands. Equally importantly, there's a lot of environmental initiatives coming out of this group. And to mention things like water sensitive urban design, which again is key to improving outcomes and can be delivered through our planning instruments to assist us in that process. Also, they've been working on infrastructure contributions by working with the state government and local councils to try and enhance and focus those planning agreements and tools on improving, again, the water quality outcomes. There was a report on the master plan delivery engine update, which is the way that they keep track of what's happening within the master plan, which has 10 key outcomes it's looking for in developing. And I'd urge anybody who, oh my goodness, my computer's going to close down. Anybody that wants to find out more about that to go onto their website and you can look at the delivery engine and you get updates on where they are in a range of different projects, which are being conducted. And at the moment they're working on two more swim, or three swim spots within the Parramatta River. They're working on things like tools to be able to report on the quality within those systems. They're working with universities to provide a better understanding of what our fauna and flora is within that catchment area and working with councils, indigenous representatives or officers to try and piece together a much more coherent and inclusive arrangement with their knowledge and how we move forward with our waterway. And equally interesting at the meeting, Professor Bruce Tom, who's the head of the Coastal Council, gave a very interesting discussion on what is happening from the Coastal Council's point of view and the government's direction to not just look at individual parts of catchments, but to have a much more integrated outcome for catchments. And so the Parramatta River Group is now going to work closely with the Catchment Management Program to ensure that there's a continuation down through the catchment and into those water bodies. The government has a desire to have a more integrated process to these. So I'd happily report to council that I think council is getting good value for its contribution to this group. It's also getting good cooperation with other parts of local government and state government in tools that can assist us in doing our business effectively and equally importantly, protecting our environment and our waterways, which we have quite a fair share of our municipality fronting onto and influencing those areas. So I commend the report to council and I think it is extremely worthwhile and beneficial process for not only Huddersfield Council, but the broader Sydney community.
